article.title: Brian Karem on Racism, Trump, and Why American Journalism Must Be Rebuilt
article.author: Sharon Kyle
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Brian Karem has spent much of his professional life asking questions that powerful people would rather not answer. He's questioned presidents, challenged government officials, gone to jail to protect a confidential source, and taken Donald Trump to court over his White House press credentials. But when I recently sat down with Karem for what was supposed to be an informal conversation, I was interested in something beyond his reputation as a combative journalist. I wanted to know what made him that way. More specifically, I wanted to understand whether his experiences had shaped his views about race, power, and the institutions that govern American life. At LA Progressive, we have long maintained that America's racial hierarchy is not some peripheral problem that can be addressed after we solve our economic and political challenges. It is central to understanding why American democracy has never fully delivered on its promises. Karem's personal history offered an unexpected starting point for that discussion. Growing Up Different in the American South Karem was born in Louisville, Kentucky, into a family with Lebanese roots on his father's side. Growing up in the South, he experienced the hostility directed at people who didn't fit neatly into America's racial categories. He recalled being subjected to anti-Arab slurs and learning early that prejudice was not an abstraction. But his family's response to racial injustice may have been even more influential than the discrimination he experienced. His grandfather, a Kentucky judge, knew Muhammad Ali and had a personal relationship with the legendary boxer. Karem told me that his family helped Ali navigate conflicts with the people controlling his early boxing career. He also recalled a revealing confrontation between his grandfather and a neighbor who insisted on calling Ali by his former name, Cassius Clay. His grandfather refused to tolerate it. As Karem remembered the exchange, his grandfather insisted that every person had the right to determine what they would be called. Anyone unwilling to respect Ali's chosen name was no longer welcome in his home. It was a small but consequential lesson about dignity, self-determination, and the importance of refusing to participate in another person's degradation. Karem also described meeting Ali as a nine-year-old participating in a Louisville boxing program. Ali visited the young boxers, and Karem had an opportunity to shadowbox with the heavyweight champion. The encounter left a lasting impression. Karem grew up in the same city that produced both Ali and journalist Hunter S. Thompson. Looking back, he sees those two figures, along with his parents, as important influences on his willingness to challenge authority. Ali demonstrated that one could stand up to powerful institutions without surrendering one's identity. Thompson showed that journalism could be irreverent, confrontational, and unwilling to accept official narratives. Those influences helped shape Karem's understanding of his profession. The Journalist's Job Is Not to Make Presidents Comfortable Karem's first experience questioning a president came during George H. W. Bush's administration. He told me that asking that question cost him his job. His confrontations with Donald Trump produced a different outcome: litigation over his press credentials. Karem takes considerable satisfaction in having prevailed in court. He describes his record against Trump as three victories and no defeats. But he rejects the notion that challenging a president constitutes rudeness. He considers it the fundamental responsibility of a journalist. Early in his White House career, Karem encountered two legendary reporters, Helen Thomas and Sam Donaldson. Thomas impressed upon him the importance of asking questions even when officials refuse to provide meaningful answers. Simply putting an issue before the president establishes that the question has been raised. Donaldson encouraged him to learn from the experience of the veteran reporters surrounding him. Together, they helped shape a philosophy Karem has carried throughout his career. The White House press secretary's responsibility, he explained, is to present the administration in the most favorable light possible. The journalist's responsibility is entirely different. It is to hold government accountable to the people. Karem also offered a definition of journalism that deserves serious consideration: good journalism, he said, is the application of the scientific method to mass communication. Journalists will make mistakes. They will sometimes get facts wrong. But the obligation is to investigate, correct errors, and continue pursuing verifiable information. For Karem, public officials are not our rulers. They are our employees. And employees must answer to the people who pay their salaries. Race, Class, and the Politics of Division Our conversation eventually returned to the subject that had prompted much of my interest in interviewing him. Race. Karem readily acknowledged the destructive influence of racism and misogyny in American political life. But he situated both within a larger economic struggle. His argument was that the wealthy benefit when working people are divided against one another. Poor white Americans, he observed, have far more material interests in common with poor Black Americans than with the wealthy people who dominate the economy. Yet racial hostility and other divisions can prevent people from recognizing those shared interests. It was a familiar argument, but one that raised an important question for me. Does economic inequality explain racial hierarchy, or has racial hierarchy been one of the principal mechanisms through which economic inequality has been created and sustained? The distinction matters. America's history of slavery, segregation, exclusion from property ownership, discriminatory lending, and unequal access to political power cannot be understood simply as unfortunate byproducts of class inequality. Race has helped determine who could accumulate wealth, whose labor could be exploited, whose rights could be violated, and whose suffering could be disregarded. Karem and I did not fully resolve that question. But his recognition that racial and economic divisions are deeply intertwined provided common ground for a broader discussion about democracy. Protest Is Not Enough Karem was particularly animated when discussing political participation. He has covered demonstrations involving thousands of people, including the No Kings protests. He described people traveling long distances, making signs, and devoting entire days to expressing their opposition to government policies. Yet he has encountered protesters who do not vote. That contradiction frustrates him. He believes demonstrations matter, but they must be accompanied by sustained political participation. Voting, organizing, helping others reach polling places, and even running for office are among the tools Americans have available to exercise political power. I agreed with the larger point. LA Progressive exists in part because we believe political outrage must be connected to understanding, organization, and action. It is not enough to identify what is wrong with the system. We must also develop alternatives and work toward implementing them. Karem emphasized that Americans too often forget the degree of power they possess collectively. He worries that political alienation has become so pronounced that some people are willing to entertain authoritarian alternatives when democratic institutions fail to deliver. His answer is not to abandon democracy, but to make it more responsive and accessible. He also believes schools must restore serious attention to civics and the social sciences. That brought us naturally to the institution that has occupied most of his professional life. Journalism. The Billionaire Problem in American Media When I asked Karem about his book, Free the Press: The Death of American Journalism and How to Revive It , his answer was immediate. Break up the media monopolies. Karem believes concentrated corporate ownership is among the principal reasons American journalism has deteriorated. He recalled entering a profession in which experienced reporters learned their craft over many years, often beginning in local newsrooms before moving into national reporting. Today, he argued, major media companies frequently prioritize lower labor costs, audience metrics, and access to powerful officials over the experience and independence required for serious reporting. He was especially critical of journalists who view proximity to the president as a professional achievement rather than a potential threat to their independence. He described some White House reporters as functioning like stenographers or public relations representatives rather than independent investigators. Karem also challenged the obsession with viral moments and performative confrontation. A provocative question designed to generate attention is not necessarily a question designed to produce useful information. His criticism extended beyond traditional news organizations to the technology companies that control digital distribution. Independent publishers may own their publications, but they remain dependent on a relatively small number of platforms to reach audiences. That concentration of power creates another form of vulnerability. Karem proposed several reforms: stronger limits on media ownership, tax incentives for independent publishers, low-interest financing, support for hiring local reporters, and renewed public-interest obligations for broadcasters. He also advocated restoring the Fairness Doctrine, which once imposed certain obligations on broadcasters to address controversial public issues. These proposals would require substantial policy debate. But his central argument was unmistakable. Journalism cannot become genuinely independent if its economic survival remains controlled by a handful of powerful corporations. For those of us operating independent publications, that argument is more than theoretical. It describes the environment in which we work every day. Facts, Truth, and the Responsibility of Journalism One of Karem's most interesting observations concerned the distinction between facts and truth. He does not believe journalists should appoint themselves arbiters of everyone's ultimate truth. Instead, he believes their responsibility is to provide carefully verified factual information from which people can form their own conclusions. That distinction struck me as particularly relevant to the present media environment. Political debate increasingly takes place among people who do not share a common factual foundation. Competing interpretations of events are inevitable in a democracy. But democratic deliberation becomes nearly impossible when citizens cannot agree on what actually happened. Karem sees propaganda, concentrated media ownership, and the erosion of professional standards as major contributors to that problem. He also connects the current media environment to political and regulatory decisions made over several decades, particularly during the Reagan era. Our conversation touched on the Powell memorandum, the conservative political realignment of the late twentieth century, and the dismantling of regulatory structures that once placed greater limits on media concentration. Karem sees these developments as interconnected. His larger concern is that the public has lost access to the independent reporting necessary to understand who exercises power and how that power is used. A Documentary and a Warning About Democracy Karem is also promoting a documentary, The First 100 Days , examining the early period of Trump's second administration and the political response that followed. He told me the film explores the administration's actions, their consequences for civil liberties, and the public dissatisfaction that contributed to the 2026 midterm election results. He was particularly concerned about the need for congressional oversight. But he also warned against treating the election as a permanent political realignment that requires no further work. Voters may have delivered a rebuke to the administration, he argued, but elected officials must respond to the underlying grievances that motivated them. Otherwise, the same frustration could eventually turn against the politicians who benefited from it. He repeatedly returned to the need to distinguish accountability from political retaliation. As he put it, "The divisiveness has to stop. The call for justice should never end." That distinction deserves attention. Accountability should not depend on which political party holds power. It should depend on whether public officials have fulfilled their obligations and respected the rights of the people they serve. What Muhammad Ali, Helen Thomas, and Brian Karem Have in Common As our conversation drew to a close, I found myself thinking about the people Karem had identified as influences on his life. Muhammad Ali refused to surrender his identity to satisfy the expectations of others. Helen Thomas insisted that journalists ask questions even when the powerful would prefer silence. Sam Donaldson demonstrated that reporters must maintain their independence from the officials they cover. Karem has attempted to carry those lessons into his own work. But perhaps the most revealing part of our conversation was his insistence that journalism belongs to the public. It is not the private possession of corporate executives, wealthy investors, or government officials. Its democratic purpose is to provide the information people need to govern themselves. That mission is particularly important for communities whose experiences have historically been excluded, minimized, or distorted by dominant institutions. If journalism is to fulfill its promise, it must do more than challenge presidents. It must examine the racial and economic hierarchies that determine whose voices are heard, whose experiences are believed, and whose interests are protected. Karem's career demonstrates one form of resistance to institutional power. The challenge for independent journalism is to turn that resistance into something durable: a media system capable of informing the public, exposing abuses, and helping communities exercise meaningful democratic power. Near the end of our conversation, Karem expressed his support for independent publications like LA Progressive. He urged audiences to support local journalists and community-based news organizations, describing community journalism as the backbone of the profession. His message was simple. If we want journalism to survive, we must support the people and institutions doing the work. And if we want democracy to survive, we must ensure that journalism remains capable of holding power accountable. That is a mission LA Progressive can recognize. Brian Karem is a veteran White House correspondent, author of Free the Press: The Death of American Journalism and How to Revive It, and host of the Just Ask the Question podcast. His documentary, The First 100 Days, examines the opening period of Donald Trump's second administration. This article is adapted from a conversation with LA Progressive publisher Sharon Kyle.
